questions.prompt: Why does @Published alone not enable KVO? Who must own the observed model and registration, and where may callbacks run?
questions.scenario: A synthetic settings controller gets no KVO updates. A later revision keeps delivering updates after that controller’s intended lifetime.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin StateFlow and Java listeners help distinguish a value source from registration lifetime. Neither implements Objective-C selector dispatch, KVO interception, or UIKit main-thread delivery.
rubric: Uses an NSObject subclass with an @objc dynamic property for this automatic KVO case.
Separates KVO from Combine @Published and Swift Observation.
Gives the model and returned observation token deliberate owners.
Separates weak capture from explicitly retiring the registration.
Handles synchronous initial delivery and does not assume MainActor scheduling.
questions.answerHTML:
KVO, or key-value observing, watches supported property changes through the Objective-C runtime. For the lesson's automatic Swift case, use an NSObject subclass and an @objc dynamic property. @objc exposes the property; dynamic keeps runtime method dispatch so KVO can intercept supported changes. @Published supplies Combine behavior and does not independently establish that KVO contract. Selector dispatch chooses an implementation from the receiver at runtime; it is not how every Swift operation is dispatched.

The controller must keep both its model and observation token alive for the chosen scope. The token is the registration handle. If its token's closure strongly captures the same controller, that ownership graph can retain the controller. A weak capture addresses that edge, while explicit invalidation addresses the registration scope. These are different fixes. Prepare all callback dependencies before registering with .initial because delivery can occur before observe returns and before the token property assignment finishes.

KVO does not automatically schedule callbacks on MainActor. Check where the source changes its value. The companion confines writers to UIKit's main thread; a different source needs serialization and a safe UI hop with freshness checks. Test initial/new delivery, invalidation, owner disappearance, and replacement of a nested observed object separately.
followUps: What must the controller initialize before registering an observation that delivers .initial synchronously?
What lifetime and freshness checks are needed if a callback forwards copied values into an async task?
pitfalls: Treating @Published, @Observable and KVO as interchangeable ways to register observation.
Expecting weak capture to end a registration or schedule callbacks safely for UI access.

questions.prompt: Why does a clear overlay steal taps, and why does a double tap also commit the single-tap action? Explain the separate routing fixes.
questions.scenario: A synthetic panel overlays a button. A neighboring pad has single- and double-tap recognizers. Reset is a target-action command with a nil target.
questions.androidBridge: Android dispatchTouchEvent/interception supplies routing vocabulary. UIKit hit testing, responder-chain target-action, and recognizer failure dependencies are separate mechanisms rather than one equivalent interception callback.
rubric: Explains hit testing in local coordinates and why clear drawing can still win the hit.
Returns nil only for the pass-through overlay itself while preserving interactive children.
Makes single require double to fail and explains the added wait for a single tap.
Avoids failure cycles and separates simultaneous-recognition policy.
Explains nil-target Reset through the installed responder hierarchy.
Requires separate touch, keyboard and accessibility interaction checks.
questions.answerHTML:
Hit testing chooses which eligible view receives a touch at a point. Check the overlay’s bounds and eligibility first. Clear drawing does not make its default hit test return nil. The lab calls super.hitTest and returns nil only when the hit is the overlay itself, preserving any real child control. Convert coordinates when delegating to another view. Do not infer empty space from private SwiftUI layer topology as a reusable platform guarantee.

The single-tap recognizer must wait for the double-tap recognizer to fail. Use single.require(toFail: double). That directed wait delays single recognition while the double remains possible; a successful double makes the single fail. The reverse edge gives the wrong precedence, and both edges create a cycle. Simultaneous recognition permission is a separate policy and does not remove the failure requirement. Check recognizer touch-cancellation behavior if controls stop receiving events.

A nil target on Reset asks UIKit to search responders for one that handles the action selector. This is responder routing, a separate mechanism from touch hit testing. It does not repeat geometric hit testing or require a global controller reference. Keep its action signature and containing controller hierarchy valid. Verify overlay pass-through, only one double-tap commit, Reset resolution, and semantic accessible button activation on a running destination. Compilation establishes signatures, not those interactions.
followUps: How should pass-through behavior preserve an interactive child added to the overlay?
How would a continuous drag’s cancellation and terminal state differ from a tap?
pitfalls: Reversing the failure dependency or adding both directions and creating a cycle.
Treating responder search, touch hit testing and VoiceOver focus as one route.

questions.prompt: An explicit position animation snaps back when it ends. How would you set the lasting model position, retarget it and freeze it safely?
questions.scenario: A synthetic CALayer moves between two endpoints. An opposite command can arrive before the current animation finishes.
questions.androidBridge: Android ObjectAnimator can update a View property over time. Core Animation presentation can move while its model already holds the destination, so target-property observations are not interchangeable.
rubric: Separates model destination, optional visible presentation sample and private render machinery.
Copies the presentation position before removing the owned animation.
Writes the model destination with implicit actions disabled.
Adds a keyed explicit animation from the copied sample to that destination.
Defines freeze versus finish and a fallback when no presentation exists.
Rejects permanent fill mode as a substitute for correct model state.
questions.answerHTML:
CABasicAnimation can move what is drawn without changing the layer’s lasting model position. When it ends, the unchanged model can make the layer snap back. Set the layer's model position to the endpoint inside a transaction with implicit actions disabled, then install the explicit position animation. Once the animation disappears, the correct model endpoint remains. Action suppression prevents accidental implicit interpolation but still permits explicitly adding an animation.

To retarget, first copy presentation()?.position, the available sample of the animated position. Do this before removing the old named animation. If no presentation exists, use a documented model fallback. Retire the old travel key, assign the new model destination, and add the new animation from the copied sample to that destination in the same bounded transaction. Core Animation copies the added animation; editing the local object afterward does not edit the installed copy.

Freeze means stop where it appears now. Finish means keep the intended endpoint. They require different model writes. Freeze writes the pre-removal visible sample into the model and removes travel. Finish removes travel while preserving the already-written endpoint. fillMode forwards with removal disabled can conceal an incorrect model and is not the repair. Verify interruption, resizing, leaving the view, and Reduce Motion independently. A successful build cannot prove a sampled value corresponded to a particular displayed frame.
followUps: Which model fallback should freeze use when there is no presentation representation yet?
How could a resize preserve semantic animation progress instead of merely clamping position?
pitfalls: Removing the animation before copying the presentation sample.
Keeping isRemovedOnCompletion = false instead of setting the correct model endpoint.

questions.prompt: The full feed hitches, although its shimmer looks smooth alone. How would you distinguish delayed app commits from expensive rendering?
questions.scenario: Without recording a frame trace, a synthetic team proposes CATransaction.flush after every scroll event.
questions.androidBridge: Android RenderThread and frame scheduling suggest independent preparation/render costs. UIKit/Core Animation do not expose the same Choreographer or SurfaceFlinger contracts, and coroutine completion is not frame presentation.
rubric: Defines the workload, observable frame problem and named measurement destination.
Separates main-thread preparation and commit delays from rendering and composition cost.
Rejects a flush change made without supporting evidence.
Compares alternatives and names investigation and rollback owners.
Keeps Reduce Motion and interaction-correctness gates.
Separates source inspection, compilation, recorded traces and measured results.
questions.answerHTML:
A shimmer looking smooth alone tells you only about that isolated case. It does not identify why the full feed hitches. Define the failing workload: fixture list size, images, scroll path, window size, text size, destination, and warm/cold conditions. Capture representative frame hitches and relevant main-thread work rather than deriving performance from source or animation duration. App preparation and transaction submission can be delayed; render composition can also miss deadlines after a timely commit.

Check whether app-side layout, state updates or image preparation delay submission. Separately check rendering costs such as masks, effects and drawing overlapping content, called overdraw. A presentation-layer sample is useful for retargeting but is not a frame trace. CATransaction.flush is not a justified per-event fix and can alter batching without solving the cause.

Name who reproduces the workload and who owns the limited implementation experiment. Compare alternatives such as reducing preparation work or simplifying the expensive visual effect, preserve the baseline, and specify a rollback switch. Verify cancellation, latest-command model state, Reduced Motion, and accessible activation alongside timing. Report which traces were actually captured and which remain pending. The course's inspected shimmer and compiled lab are source/API evidence; neither supplies device measurements for this feed.
followUps: Which trace finding would justify changing shimmer rather than image preparation?
What baseline, representative-device evidence and rollback would be required before several teams adopt the change?
pitfalls: Calling source-reading hypotheses measured GPU findings.
Treating transaction completion, async completion and a frame actually appearing on display as the same event.

questions.prompt: A wrapping Layout caches only child count and top-aligns mixed fonts. What must its cache check, and where should it place the baselines in LTR and RTL?
questions.scenario: Children measure 40×20 with baseline 15 and 50×30 with baseline 20. Offered width changes from 120 to 70. The item gap is 8 and row gap is 12.
questions.androidBridge: Compose measurement and placeables help describe geometry. SwiftUI proposals are not hard constraints, and layout cache callbacks do not imply Compose measurement-cache semantics.
rubric: Checks current dimensions, baselines, row-break key, width and gaps before reusing this logical arrangement.
Separates updateCache from recomputing for a changed proposal.
Calculates ascent 20, descent 10 and wide-row y offsets 5 and 0.
Calculates narrow height 62 and uses consistent measurement and placement proposals.
Passes logical x unchanged because SwiftUI flips RTL placement and must not be made to reflect it twice.
Keeps logical IDs and states container-baseline and overflow limits.
questions.answerHTML:
Two children can stay two children while their sizes or row positions change. Width, font, measured dimensions, baseline guides, row-break keys and spacing all affect this arrangement. Clear the cache in updateCache, but also compare the relevant measured inputs for the current proposal on every arrangement request. That set of inputs is the cache fingerprint. The lab remeasures current proxy dimensions and caches only the pure arrangement, so it makes no unsupported promise to eliminate text measurement cost.

Call the first child A and the second B. At width 120 they fit with an eight-point gap. Ascent is the height above the baseline: max(15,20) = 20. Descent is the height below it: max(5,10) = 10. Place A at (0,5) and B at (48,0) so both baselines reach 20; the row height is 30. At width 70 they wrap: A is at (0,0), B is at (0,32), and total height is 20 + 12 + 30 = 62. Placement should use the same capped-width, unspecified-height measurement policy, with bounds origin added afterward.

For each given width, keep those logical positions in both left-to-right and right-to-left layout. SwiftUI owns the direction change when placing subviews. SwiftUI automatically flips subview x placement in RTL; manually reflecting first would double-flip it. A numeric UnitPoint anchor does not disable that behavior. Keep logical order and IDs, and verify native RTL separately. Oversize children follow the stated overflow policy. Internal row baseline alignment does not establish an explicit container first/last baseline contract; that needs separate implementation and typography tests.
followUps: How does changing RowBreakKey invalidate arrangement without replacing a child? Why does this logical helper omit direction?
Why can using the measured response width as a placement proposal change the question asked of the child?
pitfalls: Assuming updateCache runs for every offered-width probe.
Reflecting x before SwiftUI reflects RTL placement, or reversing record identity to simulate direction.

questions.prompt: A scrolling form cannot reliably reveal an invalid field. How would you repair scrolling, keyboard focus and VoiceOver focus without mixing their owners?
questions.scenario: A synthetic vertical form contains horizontal choices and a custom baseline layout. Validation inserts an error element after editing.
questions.androidBridge: Compose nestedScroll exposes pre/post delta consumption; SwiftUI native scrolling does not provide the same callback surface. Android keyboard focus and accessibility focus are also distinct, but traversal rules still require platform-specific verification.
rubric: Chooses one vertical scroll owner and an explicit policy for the horizontal strip.
Avoids blanket zero-distance or high-priority gesture fixes.
Uses separate FocusState editing cases and AccessibilityFocusState error requests.
Uses stable current field IDs and a current scroll proxy.
Defines software and hardware keyboard, VoiceOver, large-text and RTL checks.
Names owners, alternatives and runtime behavior still unverified.
questions.answerHTML:
Choose one owner for vertical scrolling. Let the choices scroll horizontally unless a second vertical scroll area is essential. The two directions then have separate jobs. Leave native arbitration intact before adding custom gestures. A broad zero-distance or high-priority drag can steal page scrolling and still fail after cancellation. If same-axis nesting is necessary, specify its viewport, handoff, and accessible alternatives rather than translating Compose nestedScroll callbacks literally.

FocusState tracks which field receives editing input. Use one optional Field enum with a distinct case for each TextField. AccessibilityFocusState separately requests assistive focus, such as on an error element. On submit, advance to the intended field and request scrolling through the current ScrollViewReader proxy and stable field ID. Validation can clear editing focus and separately request assistive focus on an installed error element. That does not guarantee a software keyboard, announcement, or hardware Tab order.

If content still overflows, compare the custom container with a simpler stacked form. Assign a feature owner for focus/validation and a container owner for layout/arbitration. Verify diagonal drags, software submit/toolbar progression, Tab and Shift-Tab, VoiceOver reading/activation, large text, and RTL on named destinations. Keep drafts intact during cancellation. Compiler and host geometry checks are useful but do not certify those runtime outcomes.
followUps: Which attempt guard would reject a stale focus request after async validation?
What actual fling and handoff evidence is needed for same-axis nested scrolling?
pitfalls: Using one Boolean for both editing focus and assistive focus.
Calling a source assignment or ordinary-size preview proof of accessible traversal.

questions.prompt: Does every scene connection create a new session? Does every inactive phase mean background? Correct those claims and name the resource owners.
questions.scenario: The app has two windows. One is interrupted while the other stays active. Its checklist saves drafts only in applicationWillTerminate.
questions.androidBridge: Android Application/Activity/task/window concepts help enumerate owners. UIKit scene/session identity and ordinary rotation behavior do not follow Activity recreation, saved-instance-state, or task identity exactly.
rubric: Separates process, scene session, connected scene, window, controller, view and durable draft identities.
Explains that connection can restore or reconnect an existing session.
Distinguishes inactive, background, disconnection and permanent session discard.
Separates a view’s scenePhase from the App’s aggregate phase.
Rejects termination-only saving and one universal callback sequence.
Keeps per-scene presentation separate from shared account services.
questions.answerHTML:
One running app process can share services across windows. Each scene separately owns its navigation and presentation. UISceneSession identifies a persistent interaction session. A connected UIScene, its windows and its controllers are the live UI objects for that session. scene(_:willConnectTo:options:) can create or restore an interface for an existing session, so it is not a new-session test. Disconnection is also different from permanently discarding that session.

Inactive can mean a temporary interruption. It does not always mean the scene entered the background. Reactivation therefore need not include a background-to-foreground callback. A view's scenePhase reflects its containing scene, while an App-level phase aggregates scenes and can stay active while another window is inactive. Quiet the affected visual work without indiscriminately cancelling a shared account service used elsewhere.

A controller disappearing, a View description being rebuilt, the process launching and a durable draft being deleted are different lifetime events. SwiftUI view descriptions can change while identity-associated state survives. Preserve important drafts through normal durable commits: a suspended process may terminate without applicationWillTerminate. The familiar launch/foreground/active path is illustrative rather than universal. Use WindowGroup for scene roots and one delegate adaptor for needed process-level callbacks, then verify actual routes and transitions on a destination.
followUps: Who should own a field’s focus request, and who should own the authenticated repository shared across scenes?
How can an existing scene session reconnect while its durable document outlives both controller instances?
pitfalls: Deleting a durable draft when sceneDidDisconnect runs.
Assuming interruption or rotation repeats the full launch sequence.

questions.prompt: How should incoming routes compete with restoration on cold and warm starts? How can an expiring checkpoint reject old account and attempt callbacks?
questions.scenario: Restored Alpha competes with incoming Beta. An old checkpoint expires near a replacement attempt. The process can disappear before cleanup runs.
questions.androidBridge: Android intents, saved state, and coroutine generations help describe intent precedence and stale acceptance. They do not reproduce SceneStorage guarantees, UIKit background identifiers, or iOS scheduling duration.
rubric: Gives valid external intent priority over restoration and defines invalid-input policies separately.
Uses one parser and a scene-owned reducer for initial and later routes.
Checks schema, account, authorization and existence after parsing and rejects previous-account work.
Uses SceneStorage for small presentation values rather than durable drafts.
Guards completion and expiration by attempt and promptly ends only the matching background identifier.
Compares alternatives, names owners and separates host policy tests from installed delivery and expiration evidence.
questions.answerHTML:
Parse initial and later URL or activity inputs with the same strict rules. A scene-owned reducer then decides which route to accept. A valid incoming Beta should outrank stale restored Alpha. Define invalid-input behavior explicitly: this lab's cold model falls back to root, while invalid warm input preserves the current route. Restore only recognized schema and IDs, and validate the current account, authorization, and record existence before revealing protected content.

SceneStorage is for small restorable presentation values. Save important drafts through durable transactions with an interrupted-write recovery policy. Capture an account epoch around async validation so a prior account cannot commit navigation after logout. A view's later onAppear must not overwrite an already accepted external intent with stale restoration.

Before the protected work, request finite background execution and handle a rejected request. Label each attempt with a generation checked by both expiration and completion. Retirement clears acceptance, cancels work, makes the identifier invalid, and ends the old identifier once. Old callbacks must not end a replacement. The documented five-second callback budget is not a fixed grant for arbitrary async work.

Name routing and storage owners, compare immediate checkpoints with a separately scheduled durable job where appropriate, and define recovery after interrupted writes. Host tests establish parser/precedence logic; installed cold/warm delivery, actual expiration, two-window behavior, and durability require independent evidence.
followUps: What recovery applies when a route parses but authorization fails after the account changes?
Which interrupted-write check proves recovery before durable commit?
pitfalls: Letting callback arrival order accidentally decide whether restoration or external intent wins.
Calling a completed synthetic sleep or build evidence of durable background execution.
